scenario: Adopt Lintwise as a required pre-merge check (eight engineers)

motion.text: The team runs Lintwise in warn-only (advisory) mode on every monorepo PR in parallel with the existing 11-minute build for two sprints, using baseline mode to freeze legacy findings and measure false-positive rate per PR. At the end of the calibration window, the team reviews the FP-per-PR data, secret-detection verification results, and Lintwise's supply-chain dependency-tree audit. Only rules that (a) remain under one false positive per PR, (b) have a written one-line explanation and style-guide pointer in their output message, and (c) pass the security audit are promoted to blocking pre-merge checks. A written rollback path (revert to advisory, not delete) and a two-person override-with-justification hatch for production hotfixes are included in the policy document. Marcus confirms runner capacity before parallel placement goes live. If any blocking rule's FP rate later exceeds the agreed threshold, enforcement reverts to advisory for that rule pending re-tuning.

objectors.reason: The supply-chain audit of Lintwise itself is still pending and Priya's "no secrets scanner" claim directly contradicts my notes, so neither security prerequisite has been resolved and voting would mean endorsing an unvetted tool into our mandatory CI path.

The motion as written makes Lintwise an immediate blocking gate, but my support—and most colleagues'—is conditional on a warn-mode calibration window, baseline freeze, and per-PR false-positive measurement that must be encoded before it can block merges, so the current wording is missing an essential precondition for trustworthy signal.

chairQuestions.experience_sought: You reported roughly 4 minutes added to CI over six months, while Marcus and Jin expect static analysis to run in seconds. Can you confirm the exact wall-clock duration Lintwise took, and whether that 4 minutes was measured as a serial step before the build or run concurrently with it?

When you ran Lintwise on your side project, did its ruleset include any checks for hardcoded credentials, API keys, tokens, or private keys in source files, or was it limited to style, formatting, and structural-quality checks?
